overview.title: Oxford-IIIT Pets: downloading a segmentation dataset
overview.section: 11.2 Training a segmentation model from scratch
overview.main_topic: Start of the from-scratch semantic segmentation example: the task (separate the main subject from its background), the Oxford-IIIT Pets dataset and its three-valued segmentation masks, downloading and extracting it, and building sorted lists of image and mask paths.
overview.central_idea: A segmentation mask is the segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input, with one channel, where each integer is the class of the corresponding pixel. Here the values are 1 (foreground), 2 (background), and 3 (contour). Inputs and masks share filenames, so sorting both path lists pairs them up.
overview.importance: It turns the definition of semantic segmentation (p.334) into concrete data: what a target looks like, how it is stored, and how inputs are matched to targets. Everything in section 11.2 depends on these path lists and this label encoding.
learning_objectives: State what the first segmentation example will learn (subject vs background, semantic segmentation).
Describe the Oxford-IIIT Pets dataset: 7,390 cat and dog pictures with per-pixel masks.
Define a segmentation mask and its relationship to the input image.
Know the meaning of mask values 1, 2, and 3.
Explain the download, extraction, and path-listing code, including the '[!.]*.png' glob pattern.
prerequisites: Image classification datasets and labels (chapter 8; p.129 glossary)
Basic Python pathlib and shell commands in notebooks

summary:
A transition sentence proposes training a **small segmentation model from scratch** to get familiar with segmentation.

**Section 11.2** focuses on **semantic segmentation**. It uses cats and dogs again (as in chapter 8), but this time the goal is to **tell apart the main subject and its background** pixel by pixel instead of classifying the whole picture.

**11.2.1 Downloading a segmentation dataset.** The dataset is **Oxford-IIIT Pets**: 7,390 pictures of various breeds of cats and dogs, each with a segmentation mask. The book defines a **segmentation mask** as the segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the **same size as the input**, with a **single color channel**, where each integer value is the class of the corresponding input pixel. Here the values are:

- `1`: foreground
- `2`: background
- `3`: contour

The first code block uses `wget` to download `images.tar.gz` and `annotations.tar.gz`, and `tar -xf` to extract them. The leading `!` runs shell commands from a notebook cell.

Images are JPGs in `images/` (for example, `images/Abyssinian_1.jpg`). Each mask is a PNG with the **same name** in `annotations/trimaps/` (for example, `annotations/trimaps/Abyssinian_1.png`).

The second code block builds two lists with `pathlib`: `input_img_paths = sorted(input_dir.glob("*.jpg"))` and `target_paths = sorted(target_dir.glob("[!.]*.png"))`. The pattern `[!.]` excludes spurious files in the trimaps directory whose names start with a dot. Because both lists are sorted by the shared filename stem, element *i* of one corresponds to element *i* of the other.

The next pages display an example image and its mask (figures 11.3 and 11.4, pp.336-337), subtract 1 from the mask values to get labels 0-2, and resize everything to 200 × 200.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Oxford-IIIT Pets has 7,390 pictures of various cat and dog breeds, with foreground-background segmentation masks. A segmentation mask is the segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input, with one color channel, where each integer is the class of the corresponding pixel. Here, mask pixels take the values 1 (foreground), 2 (background), and 3 (contour) (bullets p335_e08 to p335_e10).

concepts.name: Segmentation mask
concepts.definition: The segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input, with a single color channel, where each integer value is the class of the corresponding pixel.
concepts.intuition: A paint-by-numbers sheet laid over the photo.
concepts.technical: Shape (H, W, 1) of integer class ids. Here the ids are 1 (foreground), 2 (background), and 3 (contour), later shifted to 0-2.
concepts.significance: It defines the target that the segmentation model must reproduce.
concepts.misconception: That the mask is an RGB color image. It has one channel of class integers, and colors only appear when you visualize it.

concepts.name: Semantic segmentation (subject vs background)
concepts.definition: Classifying each pixel into a semantic category; here into foreground, background, or contour.
concepts.intuition: Cut-out the pet from the photo, with a fuzzy border band.
concepts.significance: The task of the from-scratch model in section 11.2.
concepts.example: Telling the main subject apart from its background.
concepts.misconception: That the model will tell cats from dogs. The classes are regions, not species.

concepts.name: Oxford-IIIT Pets dataset
concepts.definition: A dataset of 7,390 pictures of various breeds of cats and dogs, with a segmentation mask for each picture.
concepts.intuition: A small, clean dataset with one pet per photo.
concepts.technical: Images are JPG files in images/, and masks are PNG files with the same name in annotations/trimaps/.
concepts.significance: Small enough to load fully into memory (p.337) and train on quickly.
concepts.misconception: That its masks are binary. They have three values, including contour.

concepts.name: Aligning inputs and targets by sorted filenames
concepts.definition: Pairing each input with its target by sorting two path lists whose files share names.
concepts.intuition: Two decks of cards sorted the same way so that card i of each deck matches.
concepts.technical: sorted(glob('*.jpg')) and sorted(glob('[!.]*.png')) produce lists in the same order because the stems are identical. Hidden files must be filtered or the lists shift by one.
concepts.example: Index 9 of both lists is displayed together on p.336.
concepts.misconception: That glob returns files in a guaranteed order. It does not, which is why sorted() is used.

code.title: Listing input and target file paths
code.original_code:
import pathlib

input_dir = pathlib.Path("images")
target_dir = pathlib.Path("annotations/trimaps")

input_img_paths = sorted(input_dir.glob("*.jpg"))
target_paths = sorted(target_dir.glob("[!.]*.png"))
code.what_it_does: Builds two sorted lists: all JPG input images and all PNG trimap masks, ignoring hidden files in the trimaps folder, so that the two lists line up index by index.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports pathlib for object-oriented filesystem paths.
Paths to the input folder and the mask folder.
All .jpg files in images/, sorted by name (which also groups them by breed).
All .png files not starting with '.', sorted. The callout says this ignores some spurious files in the trimaps directory that start with a '.'.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the extracted folders. Output: input_img_paths and target_paths, lists of pathlib.Path objects of equal length, used on pp.336-337.
code.algorithm: Glob-match files and sort lexicographically so that matching stems align.
code.theory_link: Supervised learning needs each input paired with its target. Here the pairing comes from shared filenames.

parameters.name: "[!.]*.png"
parameters.role: Glob pattern: first character is not '.', and the name ends in .png. Excludes hidden metadata files such as '._Abyssinian_1.png'.

pitfalls: Without sorted(), glob order is filesystem-dependent and the lists can mismatch.
If any image lacks a mask (or vice versa), all later indices shift. A safer check is to compare stems: `[p.stem for p in input_img_paths] == [p.stem for p in target_paths]`.
Later shuffling must apply the same permutation to both lists (done with the same seed on p.337).

assert all(a.stem == b.stem for a, b in zip(input_img_paths, target_paths))
print(len(input_img_paths), input_img_paths[0].name, target_paths[0].name)

deeper.title: Classification label vs segmentation mask
deeper.body:
| | classification (ch. 8) | segmentation (here) |
|---|---|---|
| target per image | one integer (cat=0, dog=1) | an H × W × 1 integer image |
| values | class id | class id per pixel: 1 fg, 2 bg, 3 contour |
| storage | folder name or CSV | PNG with the same filename |
| loss (beyond the book) | crossentropy on one prediction | crossentropy averaged over all pixels |

The book's definition, 'the image segmentation equivalent of a label', is the key to this table.

deeper.title: Why a separate 'contour' class?
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the exact boundary of fur against background is hard to annotate. Pixels there are partly pet and partly background. Giving them their own class lets annotators mark a band of uncertainty instead of forcing a hard choice, and it lets the model learn where the edges are. Some practitioners merge contour into foreground or ignore it in the loss. The book keeps all three classes.

deeper.title: Why '[!.]' matters
deeper.body:
1. Archives created on macOS often contain AppleDouble files such as `._Abyssinian_1.png` next to the real ones (beyond the book; the book just says 'spurious files ... that start with a "."').
2. `glob("*.png")` matches them too, so `target_paths` would contain extra entries.
3. After sorting, these extra entries shift every subsequent target relative to its image, so the model would learn to predict the wrong masks.
4. `[!.]` in glob syntax means 'any single character except a dot', so names starting with '.' are skipped.

takeaways: Section 11.2 trains a small semantic segmentation model from scratch to separate the main subject from its background.
Oxford-IIIT Pets has 7,390 cat and dog pictures, each with a segmentation mask.
A segmentation mask is a per-pixel label: same size as the input, one channel, integer class values.
Images are images/NAME.jpg and masks are annotations/trimaps/NAME.png, so they pair by filename.
Sorted globbing aligns the two path lists, and '[!.]*.png' skips spurious hidden files.

questions.question: What does a pixel value of 3 mean in an Oxford-IIIT Pets mask?
questions.explanation: The page lists 1 (foreground), 2 (background), 3 (contour). Species is not encoded in the mask.

questions.question: How does the book define a segmentation mask?
questions.answer: The image segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input image, with a single color channel, where each integer value corresponds to the class of the corresponding input pixel.

questions.question: Why does the code use the glob pattern "[!.]*.png" for the masks?
options: To ignore spurious files in the trimaps directory whose names start with a '.'
To select only masks of cats rather than dogs
To exclude masks that contain the contour class
To sort the files by breed
questions.answer: To ignore spurious files in the trimaps directory whose names start with a '.'
questions.explanation: The callout says exactly this. The pattern does not look at species or mask contents, and sorting is done by sorted(), not by the pattern.

questions.question: Why are both path lists passed through sorted(), and what would go wrong without it?
questions.answer: Inputs and masks share filenames, so sorting both lists puts matching pairs at the same index. Without sorting, glob's filesystem-dependent order could pair images with the wrong masks, and the model would train on incorrect targets without any error.
questions.explanation: This follows from p335_e13 (same name in both folders) and the code in p335_e15.

questions.question: The input images are JPG but the masks are PNG. Why is that a sensible choice for masks?
questions.answer: PNG is lossless, so integer class values (1, 2, 3) are stored exactly. JPEG's lossy compression would create intermediate or invalid values near boundaries and corrupt the labels.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book's text, but it follows from the definition of a mask as a grid of exact integer class ids.

questions.question: What is the learning goal of the first segmentation example, and which flavor of segmentation is it?
questions.answer: To tell apart the main subject (the pet) and its background in pictures of cats and dogs. It is semantic segmentation.

questions.question: Could you write a one-line check that confirms input_img_paths and target_paths are aligned?
questions.answer: Self-check, for example: `all(a.stem == b.stem for a, b in zip(input_img_paths, target_paths)) and len(input_img_paths) == len(target_paths)`.
questions.explanation: Comparing filename stems directly checks the pairing the code relies on.
